concepts.title: Levels of EMS providers
key_points: There are four nationally recognised levels: Emergency Medical Responder, EMT, Advanced EMT and Paramedic
Each level is defined by what it is trained and licensed to do, not by the badge or the vehicle
Emergency Medical Responder: first on scene, basic life support, minimal equipment
EMT: the backbone level — assessment, airway, bleeding control, splinting, and a short list of assisted medications
Advanced EMT: EMT skills plus some advanced airways, intravenous access and a wider medication list
Paramedic: the widest scope — advanced airways, cardiac monitoring and interpretation, and a large medication list
Scope of practice is set by the state and can be narrower than the national level suggests
Knowing what the level above you can do tells you when to call for them, which is a core EMT skill
misconceptions: Assuming national levels mean the same scope everywhere
Thinking the vehicle determines the level of care
Not calling for a higher level early enough because it feels like admitting defeat

read.plain:
There are four levels of EMS provider recognised nationally, and they stack.

Emergency Medical Responder is the first rung. Often a firefighter, a police officer, or an industrial first responder. They arrive first, start basic life support, control bleeding, use an AED, and hold things together until a transporting unit arrives. Minimal equipment, enormous value.

EMT is the level this whole tier is about, and it is the backbone of the system. Full patient assessment, airway management with basic adjuncts, oxygen, ventilation, bleeding control, splinting, childbirth, and a short list of medications that are mostly assisted rather than administered independently.

Advanced EMT adds a layer: some advanced airway devices, intravenous access, and a wider medication list.

Paramedic is the widest scope. Advanced airways, cardiac monitoring and rhythm interpretation, a large medication list, and a range of procedures the levels below do not carry.

Two things matter more than memorising the list.

First, the level is about what a person is trained and licensed to do, not what vehicle they arrived in or what the patch says. An ambulance is not automatically a paramedic unit, and a fire engine may carry paramedics.

Second, scope of practice is set by your state, and it can be narrower than the national description. The national levels describe the ceiling; your state sets your actual ceiling, and your medical director may set it lower still. Learn yours specifically.

And the practical reason to know all this: recognising when you need the level above you. Calling for a paramedic early is not an admission that you cannot cope. It is a clinical decision made on the patient's behalf, and the time it takes for them to arrive is time you do not get back by waiting.
read.standard: Four nationally recognised levels of EMS provider exist, each defined by trained and licensed capability rather than by agency or vehicle type. Emergency Medical Responder provides initial basic life support with minimal equipment. Emergency Medical Technician provides comprehensive assessment, basic airway management, oxygen administration, ventilation, haemorrhage control, immobilisation, obstetric care and a limited formulary administered principally by assistance. Advanced Emergency Medical Technician adds selected advanced airway devices, intravenous access and an expanded formulary. Paramedic holds the broadest scope, including advanced airway management, cardiac monitoring and interpretation, and extensive pharmacological and procedural capability. Scope of practice is determined by state licensure and may be narrower than the national level description, with medical direction potentially narrowing it further. Recognition of the need for a higher level of care, and early request for it, constitutes a core competency at EMT level.

eli_new.analogy: The levels are a set of nested boxes. Each one contains everything in the box below it, plus more.
eli_new.body: The practical use of this concept is not naming the levels. It is recognising the patient who needs the level above you, and calling early — because the twenty minutes a paramedic takes to arrive is twenty minutes you cannot get back by hesitating.

story.title: Call them now
story.dispatch: Medic 4 — EMT crew on scene, patient deteriorating, paramedic unit 18 minutes out.
story.body:
The EMT in charge asked for the paramedic unit four minutes after arriving, before anything had clearly gone wrong, and felt slightly foolish doing it.

They arrived at the same moment things did go wrong.

Eighteen minutes is eighteen minutes whether you ask at minute four or minute twenty. Only one of those gets them there in time.

concepts.title: Components of an EMS system and medical direction
key_points: An EMS system is more than ambulances: it includes access (the emergency number), dispatch, first response, transport, hospitals, rehabilitation and the training that feeds it
Every EMT works under the licence of a physician medical director — you do not practise on your own authority
Offline medical direction is the standing orders and protocols written in advance, which cover most of what you do
Online medical direction is contacting a physician in real time for a decision that is not covered, or that protocol requires you to ask about
Protocols are the default answer; a phone call is for the question the protocol did not anticipate
Quality improvement closes the loop by reviewing what actually happened and changing the protocols that need changing
The system only works if each part hands over cleanly to the next
misconceptions: Thinking the ambulance is the EMS system
Believing you practise on your own licence
Calling medical direction for something a standing order already covers
Not calling when protocol requires it

read.plain:
An EMS system is not a fleet of ambulances. It is a chain, and the ambulance is one link.

It starts with access — somebody being able to reach help, which means an emergency number that works and is answered. Then dispatch, which decides what goes and gives instructions to the caller while it travels. Then first response, often a fire crew or police arriving before a transporting unit. Then transport. Then the hospital, and after it, rehabilitation and whatever the patient's recovery needs.

Behind all of it sits training, licensing, equipment standards, communications infrastructure, and money. And around it, quality improvement, which is the part that examines what actually happened and changes the things that need changing.

The chain matters because it is only as good as its weakest link and its worst handover. A brilliant crew who hand over badly have lost most of what they gained.

Now the part that surprises new EMTs: you do not practise on your own authority. You practise under the licence of a physician — your medical director. Everything you are permitted to do is an extension of that physician's licence, delegated to you.

That delegation comes in two forms.

Offline medical direction is written in advance: your protocols, standing orders, and guidelines. They cover the overwhelming majority of what you do, and they exist so that you do not have to phone somebody to give oxygen. When you follow a protocol, you are following a physician's instruction that was written before the call.

Online medical direction is talking to a physician in real time. You use it when protocol requires it, when a situation is not covered, or when you need a decision above your standing orders. Some protocols specify a call before a particular medication or before a refusal.

The practical rule is simple. The protocol is the default answer. The phone call is for the question the protocol did not anticipate — not for reassurance about something already written down, and not skipped when the protocol says to make it.
read.standard: An EMS system comprises public access, emergency medical dispatch, first response, transport, definitive hospital care, rehabilitation, and the supporting infrastructure of training, licensure, equipment standards, communications and funding. System performance depends on the integrity of each component and on the quality of transitions between them. Quality improvement provides retrospective review and prospective protocol modification. EMT practice occurs under delegated physician authority through a medical director rather than under independent licensure. Offline medical direction comprises protocols, standing orders and guidelines authored in advance, governing the majority of prehospital care. Online medical direction comprises real-time physician consultation, indicated where protocol requires it, where the presentation falls outside written guidance, or where an intervention exceeds standing orders. Protocols constitute the default authority; real-time consultation addresses circumstances not anticipated by written guidance and is neither substituted for protocol nor omitted where protocol mandates it.

eli_new.analogy: You are not practising medicine. You are practising a physician's medicine, at a distance, using instructions they wrote before they knew who the patient would be.
eli_new.body: The bit that catches people out is realising the protocol IS the doctor's instruction. Following a standing order is not doing something on your own — it is doing what the physician already told you to do. Which is why the call is for the thing they did not anticipate, and why skipping a required call is skipping an instruction.

story.title: It was already written down
story.dispatch: Debrief — new EMT, first week, oxygen administration.
story.body:
He stood with the mask in his hand asking whether somebody should phone the doctor first.

The standing order covering it had been signed by that doctor eighteen months earlier.

Following a protocol is not acting alone. It is doing what the physician already told you to do, before they knew who you would be doing it to.

concepts.title: Roles, responsibilities and professionalism
key_points: The EMT's first responsibility is personal safety, then the safety of the crew, the patient and bystanders — in that order
That order is not callous: an injured EMT stops being a rescuer and becomes a second patient
Core responsibilities are assessment, treatment within scope, safe transport, and an accurate handover and record
Professionalism shows in appearance, language, punctuality, confidentiality and how you speak about patients when they cannot hear you
Patient advocacy means acting in the patient's interest, including when that is inconvenient or unpopular
Continuing education is a responsibility, not an optional extra, because practice changes
You represent the service to every person on scene, and most of what they remember is how you behaved
misconceptions: Putting the patient's safety above your own
Treating professionalism as being about uniform alone
Speaking dismissively about patients out of their hearing
Treating continuing education as a box to tick

read.plain:
The EMT's responsibilities start with an order of priority that sounds wrong the first time you hear it: yourself, then your crew, then the patient, then bystanders.

It is not callousness. An injured EMT does not help anybody — they become a second patient, they occupy the resources that were coming for the first one, and the person you were trying to reach is now further from help than before you arrived. Protecting yourself first is the only version of this job that works.

After that, the core of the role: assess the patient properly, treat within your scope, transport safely to the right place, and hand over accurately with a record that matches what you did.

Professionalism is the word that gets reduced to uniform and boots, and it is much more than that. It is being on time. It is how you speak to a frightened person and to their family. It is keeping confidences. It is doing the same job well at four in the morning as at four in the afternoon.

And it is how you talk about patients when they cannot hear you. Crew rooms and ambulance cabs are where professionalism actually gets tested, because nobody is watching. How a crew speaks about a patient in private shapes how they treat the next one.

Patient advocacy means acting in the patient's interest, including when it is inconvenient. Asking for a paramedic when it will delay you. Insisting on a trauma centre that is further away. Pushing back, politely, when somebody wants to do something that is not in this person's interest. Advocacy is easy when it costs nothing, and it is only really advocacy when it costs something.

Continuing education is part of the job rather than an addition to it. What was correct teaching ten years ago is in several places now known to be wrong — backboards, ventilation rates, tourniquets. If you stop learning, your practice quietly becomes out of date while feeling exactly as confident as it always did.

And a small thing that is not small: you represent the service to every person on that scene. Most of them will not remember what you did clinically. They will remember whether you were kind.
read.standard: EMT responsibilities are ordered by priority: personal safety, crew safety, patient safety, bystander safety. This sequence reflects that provider injury converts a rescuer into an additional patient, consuming resources and delaying care. Core responsibilities comprise patient assessment, treatment within scope of practice, safe transport to an appropriate destination, and accurate handover and documentation. Professionalism encompasses appearance, punctuality, communication, confidentiality, consistency of performance, and conduct outside patient observation. Patient advocacy denotes acting in the patient's interest irrespective of convenience, including requesting additional resources, selecting a more distant appropriate facility, and challenging decisions contrary to patient interest. Continuing education constitutes an ongoing professional obligation, as practice evolves and previously accepted teaching is superseded. Providers represent their service to all persons present on scene.

eli_new.analogy: An injured EMT is not a hero. They are a second patient, and the ambulance that was coming for the first one is now needed twice.
eli_new.body: The priority order feels wrong until you picture it going wrong. You step into traffic to reach somebody, and now there are two patients, one crew, and one ambulance. The order exists so that the maths works.

story.title: Two patients
story.dispatch: Incident review — pedestrian struck, responder injured on scene.
story.body:
He crossed a live carriageway to reach her because she was lying in the road and it felt unthinkable not to.

A second vehicle came through before the road was closed.

The ambulance that was coming for her was now needed for two, and she waited longer than she would have if he had waited ninety seconds.

concepts.title: Quality improvement and evidence-based practice
key_points: Quality improvement is the system looking at what it actually did and changing what needs changing
It is built on the patient care report, so a poor record makes the whole process blind
It is about systems rather than blame — a process that lets a good clinician make an error will let the next one make it too
Evidence-based practice means treatments are used because they have been shown to work, not because they have always been done
Several long-standing EMS practices have been reversed by evidence: routine backboarding, high-dose oxygen for everyone, tourniquets as a last resort
A practice being traditional is not evidence that it works, and the fact that a patient recovered does not prove what you did helped
Research participation and honest reporting of what happened are how the evidence gets better
Being willing to say a technique you were taught has been superseded is a professional skill
misconceptions: Treating quality improvement as fault-finding
Writing a vague report and assuming nobody reads it
Defending a practice because it has always been done
Concluding an intervention worked because the patient improved
exam_favorites: Why the report underpins the process

read.plain:
Quality improvement is the part of an EMS system that looks at what the system actually did, rather than what it intended to do, and changes what needs changing.

It runs on your documentation. Every review, every audit, every protocol change starts from patient care reports, and a vague report makes the whole process blind. 'Patient treated and transported' tells the system nothing, and it tells it nothing on a scale of thousands of calls.

The principle underneath it is systems rather than blame. When something goes wrong, the useful question is not who made the error but what made the error possible — because a process that let a competent, careful person make a mistake at four in the morning will let the next competent, careful person make it too. Blame stops people reporting things, and a system where nobody reports anything cannot improve.

Evidence-based practice is the other half. It means treatments are used because somebody has shown they work, not because they have always been done.

This matters more in EMS than people expect, because several practices that were taught confidently for decades have been reversed. Every trauma patient strapped to a rigid board — reversed, because the harms turned out to be real and the benefit was not demonstrated. High-concentration oxygen for every patient regardless of saturation — reversed. Tourniquets as a desperate last resort that would cost the limb — reversed, and reversed hard.

Each of those was taught by good people who believed it. What changed was the evidence.

Which gives you two habits worth building. First, a practice being traditional is not evidence it works; 'we have always done it this way' is a description, not a justification. Second — and this is the harder one — the fact that a patient got better does not prove what you did helped. Most patients improve. Individual cases feel like proof and are not, which is exactly why the evidence has to come from more than one story.

And finally, being able to say that something you were taught has been superseded, without feeling it as a personal defeat, is a genuine professional skill. Your practice will be revised during your career. The only question is whether you revise with it.
read.standard: Quality improvement comprises systematic review of delivered care with subsequent modification of practice, protocol and process. It is dependent on patient care report data; incomplete documentation renders the process ineffective at scale. The governing principle is systems analysis rather than individual attribution, on the basis that a process permitting error by a competent provider will permit recurrence; punitive approaches suppress reporting and thereby prevent improvement. Evidence-based practice requires that interventions be justified by demonstrated efficacy rather than by tradition. Multiple established EMS practices have been reversed on the basis of accumulated evidence, including routine long spine board immobilisation, universal high-concentration oxygen administration, and restriction of tourniquet use to last resort. Traditional practice does not constitute evidence of efficacy, and individual patient recovery does not establish intervention efficacy, as most patients improve irrespective of intervention. Honest incident reporting and research participation constitute the mechanism by which the evidence base improves.

eli_new.analogy: Quality improvement asks what made the hole in the road, not who fell in it. The person who fell in is useful information; the hole is the problem.
eli_new.body: The hardest habit here is accepting that a patient getting better does not prove you helped. Almost everybody gets better. That is why one good outcome feels like proof and is not, and why the practices that got reversed were all defended for years by people pointing at patients who did well.

story.title: It has always worked
story.dispatch: Debrief — protocol change meeting, long spine boards withdrawn.
story.body:
A very experienced medic said he had boarded thousands of patients and not one had been paralysed by it.

That was almost certainly true. It was also true of every crew who had never boarded anybody.

Thousands of patients doing well is what happens either way, which is precisely why it took evidence rather than experience to settle it.

concepts.title: The public health role of EMS
key_points: EMS sees people and places that no other part of healthcare reaches, which makes it a public health resource as well as an emergency one
Injury prevention is part of the role: car seats, smoke alarms, fall prevention, helmet use
EMS data identifies patterns — a junction producing repeated crashes, a building producing repeated overdoses
Crews are often the first to see a public health problem emerging, because they go into homes
Frequent callers usually signal an unmet need rather than misuse, and are better answered with a plan than with irritation
Community paramedicine and referral pathways exist in many systems to address needs that transport does not solve
Prevention work is unglamorous and prevents more harm than any single call you will ever run
Recognising and reporting safeguarding concerns is part of this role
misconceptions: Seeing prevention as somebody else's job
Treating frequent callers as a nuisance rather than a signal
Assuming that transport solves the problem you were called to
Not reporting a pattern because one call seems isolated
exam_favorites: Why EMS is a public health resource

read.plain:
EMS goes where nothing else in healthcare goes. Into houses, at night, unannounced, on the worst day of somebody's life. No clinic, no hospital and no surgery sees what a crew sees.

That access is why EMS is a public health resource and not only an emergency one.

The most obvious part is injury prevention. Car seats fitted correctly. Smoke alarms that work. Removing the rug at the top of the stairs in an eighty-year-old's house. Helmets. None of it is dramatic and all of it prevents more harm, over a career, than any single call you will ever run.

The second part is data. Individual calls look random; thousands of them do not. A junction that produces crash after crash. A building that produces overdose after overdose. A postcode where children arrive at hospital with burns. EMS data makes those visible, and things get fixed because somebody noticed a pattern — but only if the reports were written well enough to see it.

Third, crews see emerging problems first. A new drug appearing in a town shows up in ambulances before it shows up anywhere official. Rising heat-related calls, a spike in respiratory illness, a cluster of falls in one sheltered housing block — the front line notices first.

Then there is the subject of frequent callers, which deserves care. Somebody calling repeatedly is almost always signalling an unmet need rather than misusing the service. Untreated mental illness. Isolation. A chronic condition nobody is managing. Poverty. Being frightened and alone at three in the morning. They are answered better with a plan — a referral, a community paramedic, a social care route — than with irritation, and irritation is the response the job pulls you towards when you are tired.

Many systems now have community paramedicine, referral pathways or non-transport options precisely for this. Know what yours has, because knowing it turns a frustrating repeat call into something you can actually do.

And safeguarding sits here too. You are in the house. You see the conditions, the other people, the state of the children and the state of the fridge. Noticing and reporting concerns is part of the public health role, and it is often the only chance anybody outside gets to notice.
read.standard: Emergency medical services access populations and environments not reached by other healthcare settings, constituting a public health resource in addition to an emergency response function. Injury prevention activity includes child restraint provision, smoke alarm programmes, falls risk reduction and protective equipment promotion, producing aggregate harm reduction exceeding that of individual response. Aggregated EMS data identifies geographic and temporal patterns — collision clusters, overdose locations, injury distributions — informing intervention, contingent on documentation quality. Prehospital providers frequently identify emerging public health phenomena earliest owing to community access. Frequent service users generally indicate unmet health or social need rather than misuse, and are more effectively addressed through referral pathways, community paramedicine or social care routes than through repeat transport. Recognition and reporting of safeguarding concerns constitutes part of this role, prehospital providers frequently being the only professionals accessing the home environment.

eli_new.analogy: A single call is a photograph. Ten thousand calls are a map, and the map shows where the holes are.
eli_new.body: The frequent caller is the test of this whole concept. Somebody who calls twenty times a year is telling you something is wrong that transport does not fix, and the useful response is a referral rather than a sigh. Knowing what pathways your service has turns that call from frustrating into solvable.

story.title: Twenty-two times
story.dispatch: Review — one address, twenty-two calls in a year.
story.body:
The crew rooms had a name for her and it was not a kind one.

A community paramedic visited once, properly, and found an untreated condition, a missed appointment three years earlier, and nobody checking on her at all.

She called twice in the following year. Nothing about her had been a misuse of anything; it had been a question nobody had answered.

concepts.title: Standard precautions and PPE selection
key_points: Standard precautions treat every patient's blood and body fluids as infectious, because you cannot tell by looking
Gloves for every patient contact, without exception
Eye protection and a gown whenever splashing is foreseeable — and put them on before you start, not halfway through
A mask for the patient is source control and protects everyone else; a mask for you is personal protection
Respiratory protection for suspected airborne infection follows your service's policy, including any fit-testing requirement
Select PPE from what you are about to do, not from what the call was given as
Hand hygiene before and after every patient, including after gloves come off, is the most effective single measure
Remove PPE in the order your service specifies, because contamination happens during removal
misconceptions: Choosing PPE from the dispatch code rather than the task
Putting on eye protection after suctioning starts
Skipping hand hygiene because gloves were worn
Removing gloves by touching the outside
exam_favorites: Hand hygiene as the most effective measure

read.plain:
Standard precautions rest on a single idea: you cannot tell by looking. Most people carrying a bloodborne infection do not know it themselves, and the tidy house and the well-dressed patient are no safer than any other. So you stop trying to judge, and you treat every patient's blood and body fluids the same way.

Gloves for every patient contact. Not most. Every.

Eye protection and a gown whenever splashing is foreseeable — and the word foreseeable is doing work there. Suctioning. Childbirth. A vomiting patient. Arterial bleeding. An agitated patient. Intubation attempts happening beside you. The rule is to dress for it before you start, because there is no putting goggles on once your hands are occupied and your face is already wet.

Masks work in two directions and it is worth being clear about which you mean. A surgical mask on a coughing patient is source control: it protects everybody else in the ambulance. A mask on you is personal protection. For a suspected airborne infection you follow your service's respiratory protection policy, which will specify the type of respirator and whether you need to have been fit-tested for it.

Now the habit that matters most in practice: choose your PPE from the task, not from the call.

Dispatch information is frequently wrong or incomplete. 'Chest pain' turns into a patient vomiting blood. 'Unwell' turns into childbirth. So the question to ask is not what the call was given as, but what you are about to do in the next two minutes — and dress for that.

Hand hygiene is the most effective single measure available to you, and the one most often skipped, usually because the next job is already waiting. Before the patient, after the patient, and after gloves come off. Gloves are not a substitute: hands get contaminated during removal routinely, which is why the removal technique matters and why your service specifies an order.

And remove PPE in that order, deliberately. Most contamination in the whole process happens in the thirty seconds when it is coming off.
read.standard: Standard precautions apply universally on the basis that transmissible infection cannot be identified by inspection and is frequently unknown to the carrier. Gloves are indicated for all patient contact. Eye protection and gowns are indicated where splash exposure is foreseeable, including suctioning, obstetric care, emesis, arterial haemorrhage and agitated patients, and are applied prior to commencement rather than during the procedure. Surgical masks applied to the patient provide source control; masks and respirators worn by providers provide personal protection. Respiratory protection for suspected airborne infection follows service policy including fit-testing requirements. PPE selection is determined by anticipated task rather than by dispatch information, which is frequently inaccurate or incomplete. Hand hygiene before and after patient contact, including following glove removal, constitutes the most effective transmission control measure and is the most frequently omitted; gloves do not substitute. PPE removal follows a specified sequence, as the majority of contamination occurs during doffing.

eli_new.analogy: You do not dress for the call you were given. You dress for the next two minutes of what your hands are about to do.
eli_new.body: The useful reframe: stop asking whether this patient looks infectious. That question has no reliable answer and asking it is how people get caught out. Ask instead what you are about to do, and dress for that.

story.title: Chest pain
story.dispatch: Medic 3 — chest pain, 60-year-old male, no other information.

Gloves went on in the doorway, which is what the call sounded like it needed.

He vomited a large volume of blood about forty seconds after they reached him.

The call was chest pain. What they were about to do was lean over a patient's face, and that is the thing to have dressed for.

concepts.title: Infectious disease transmission and exposure reporting
key_points: Transmission routes are bloodborne, airborne, droplet, and contact — direct or via a contaminated surface
Bloodborne exposure needs a route in: a needlestick, a splash to the eyes, nose or mouth, or blood into broken skin
Intact skin is an excellent barrier; blood on an ungloved but unbroken hand is not an exposure in the same way
Airborne particles stay suspended and travel; droplets fall quickly and travel a short distance
The highest-risk exposure you face is a sharps injury, and most happen after the procedure, during tidying up
If exposed: stop, wash or irrigate immediately, then report immediately
Some post-exposure treatments are time-critical, so delay removes the option rather than just delaying it
Report every exposure through your service's process, however small it seems and however busy you are
Nobody has ever been criticised for reporting an exposure too quickly
misconceptions: Delaying a report to the end of a shift
Assuming a small needlestick does not count
Not reporting out of embarrassment
Thinking blood on intact skin is the same as an exposure
exam_favorites: Why sharps injuries are highest risk

read.plain:
Infections move in four ways, and knowing which one you are dealing with tells you what protects you.

Bloodborne: the organism is in blood or certain body fluids and needs a route into you. A needle. A splash into your eyes, nose or mouth. Blood into skin that is already broken. Intact skin is an excellent barrier — blood on an unbroken hand is unpleasant and is not the same category of event as a needlestick.

Airborne: small particles that stay suspended in the air and drift. They can reach you across a room and linger after the patient has gone, which is why airborne precautions involve a proper respirator rather than a surgical mask.

Droplet: larger particles from coughing and sneezing that fall out of the air quickly and travel a short distance. A surgical mask and distance handle these.

Contact: touching the patient, or touching something the patient touched. The stretcher rail, the monitor cable, the door handle. This is the one that gets underestimated, and it is why cleaning between patients matters.

Now the exposure that should worry you most: sharps. A needlestick is the highest-risk occupational exposure you face, and the detail worth knowing is when they happen. Not during the procedure, when everyone is concentrating. Afterwards, during tidying up, often to somebody who did not use the needle and did not know it was there.

Which is why the rules are what they are: never recap, dispose of it yourself, immediately, into the container, and do not leave a sharp on a bench for someone else to find with their hand.

If you are exposed — needlestick, splash to the face, blood into broken skin — the sequence is short and it is urgent.

Stop. Wash the site with soap and water, or irrigate a splashed eye or mouth thoroughly. Then report immediately, through your service's process.

Immediately is the important word. Some post-exposure treatments have to start within hours to be effective, so a delay does not postpone the option — it removes it. Every hour you spend feeling stupid, or finishing the shift, or not wanting to make a fuss, is an hour of effectiveness gone.

And report everything, however small. Nobody in the history of this job has ever been criticised for reporting an exposure too quickly.

Droplet particles settle rapidly over short distances, addressed by surgical mask and separation. Contact transmission via equipment and environmental surfaces necessitates decontamination between patients. Sharps injury constitutes the highest-risk occupational exposure and predominantly occurs following the procedure during disposal or clearing, frequently affecting a provider other than the operator. Preventive measures comprise no recapping, immediate disposal by the user, and avoidance of sharps left on surfaces. Following exposure, the sequence is immediate washing or mucous membrane irrigation followed by immediate reporting through service process; post-exposure prophylaxis is time-dependent, so delay eliminates rather than postpones therapeutic options. All exposures are reported irrespective of apparent severity.

concepts.title: Scene safety mindset, violent scenes and hazards
key_points: Scene safety is not a box ticked on arrival — it is a continuous assessment that runs the whole call
A scene that was safe when you walked in can stop being safe while you are working
Form a general impression from the doorway before committing: how many people, where are the exits, what is in reach
Stage away and wait for law enforcement where there is violence, weapons, or a scene not yet secured
Never let yourself be cornered: know your route out and keep it clear
Pre-arrival warning signs include shouting, a hostile crowd, a scene that goes quiet as you arrive, and history at the address
Common physical hazards are traffic, unstable vehicles, fire, electricity, animals, sharps, and unsafe structures
Position the ambulance to protect the working area and to allow you to leave without reversing where possible
If it becomes unsafe, leave — you can come back with police, and you cannot come back at all if you are hurt
misconceptions: Treating scene safety as a one-off check at the door
Entering a scene because the patient sounds critical
Parking so that leaving requires a three-point turn
Staying in a deteriorating scene because you have already started treatment
exam_favorites: Staging and waiting for law enforcement

read.plain:
Scene safety gets taught as something you assess on arrival, and that framing is the problem. It is not a check. It is a continuous assessment that runs from dispatch until you are back in the vehicle.

A scene that was safe when you walked in can stop being safe. The relative who was quiet becomes agitated. The crowd outside grows. The dog gets let in. The car you are working beside is on a slope. You are looking down at a patient with your back to a room, and everything you are not watching is changing.

Start before you arrive. Dispatch information, history at that address, time of night, what you can hear as you pull up. A scene that goes quiet when you arrive is telling you something, and so is one where nobody comes out to meet you.

Then the doorway. Before you commit, take one deliberate look: how many people are here, where are the exits, what is in reach that could be used, where is the patient in relation to both. That pause costs about three seconds and it is the most useful three seconds of the call.

Where there is violence, weapons, or a scene that has not been secured, you stage away and wait for law enforcement. This is genuinely hard to do when dispatch says somebody is bleeding, and it is still the right answer. You cannot treat anybody from a hospital bed, and a crew who go in and get hurt have converted one patient into three.

Inside, do not get cornered. Know your way out and keep it clear. Do not put yourself at the far end of a room, or in a bathroom, or behind a bed with a person between you and the door. Position so that both you and the patient can leave.

The physical hazards are the more ordinary half: live traffic, vehicles that have not been stabilised, fire, electricity, animals, sharps in the house, floors and structures that are not sound. Park to protect your working area, and where you can, park so you can drive out forwards rather than reversing.

And the rule that underpins all of it: if it becomes unsafe, you leave. Not when you have finished the intervention. Not once the patient is packaged. You leave, and you come back with police. You can always come back. You cannot come back at all if you are hurt.
read.standard: Scene safety constitutes continuous assessment from dispatch through to clearance rather than a discrete arrival check, as scene conditions evolve during the encounter. Pre-arrival assessment incorporates dispatch information, address history, temporal factors and auditory cues on approach. Doorway assessment prior to entry establishes occupancy, egress routes, accessible objects and patient position. Scenes involving violence, weapons or unsecured status require staging at a distance pending law enforcement, irrespective of reported patient acuity, as provider injury multiplies casualties and removes responding capability. Providers maintain unobstructed egress and avoid positions permitting entrapment. Physical hazards include live traffic, unstabilised vehicles, fire, electrical hazards, animals, sharps and structural instability. Vehicle positioning protects the working area and permits forward egress where feasible. Deterioration in scene safety mandates withdrawal irrespective of treatment stage, with return following law enforcement securing.

eli_new.analogy: Scene safety is not a door you walk through. It is a weather report you keep checking, because it changes while you are standing in it.
eli_new.body: The hardest version of this is leaving a scene you have already started working in. Everything in you says finish what you started. The answer is that you can come back with police in four minutes, and you cannot come back at all if you are the one on the floor.

concepts.title: Stress, critical incident stress and resilience
key_points: Stress in this job is normal and expected, and the question is what you do with it rather than whether you have it
Acute stress happens during or immediately after an incident; cumulative stress builds quietly over months and years
Cumulative stress is the more dangerous of the two, because nothing identifies the moment it started
Warning signs include sleep disturbance, irritability, withdrawal, loss of interest, increased drinking, and intrusive memories
Some calls land harder than others regardless of experience: children, people you know, mass casualties, and calls that resemble your own life
Talking to somebody is a professional behaviour, not a failure of one
Peer support, employee assistance programmes and professional help exist, and knowing what yours are before you need them matters
Look after your crewmate: a colleague who has gone quiet is telling you something
The old model of mandatory debriefing after every incident is no longer applied uniformly, and approaches vary — know your service's
misconceptions: Believing that experienced providers do not find calls difficult
Waiting until you are in crisis to find out what support exists
Treating a quiet colleague as fine because they said they were
Assuming cumulative stress will resolve on its own
exam_favorites: Why cumulative stress is more dangerous

read.plain:
Stress in this job is not a sign that something has gone wrong with you. It is the predictable result of doing the job, and everybody who does it for long enough carries some. The useful question is never whether you have it, but what you do with it.

There are two shapes it takes.

Acute stress arrives with an incident: during it or immediately after. Shaking hands, a racing heart, replaying the call, difficulty sleeping that night. It is sharp, it has an obvious cause, and it usually settles.

Cumulative stress is the other one, and it is the more dangerous of the two precisely because it has no moment. It builds over months and years out of ordinary calls, none of which was the one that did it. Nobody can point to a day it started, which means nobody notices it starting — including you.

What it looks like: sleeping badly, or too much. Irritability with people who did not deserve it. Withdrawing from things you used to want to do. Losing interest. Drinking more than you used to. Intrusive memories arriving uninvited. Feeling flat, or feeling nothing at all about calls that used to affect you.

Some calls land harder than others and this is not about experience. Children, always. Somebody you know, or somebody who looks like someone you know. Mass casualty incidents. And calls that resemble your own life — the same age as your daughter, the same street you grew up on, the same car. Twenty years in the job does not protect against those, and expecting it to is how people end up thinking there is something wrong with them.

Talking to somebody is a professional behaviour. Not a failure of one. The people who last in this job are not the ones who feel less; they are the ones who deal with what they feel instead of stacking it.

Find out what support your service has before you need it — peer support, an employee assistance programme, professional counselling routes. The worst time to work out how to access help is the moment you need it.

And look after your crewmate. A colleague who has gone quiet, or who has stopped coming out, or who is drinking more, is telling you something without saying it. Asking twice is often the whole intervention.

One note on practice: the older model of mandatory formal debriefing after every significant incident is no longer applied uniformly, because the evidence for it was mixed. Approaches differ between services now. Know what yours does.
read.standard: Occupational stress is an expected consequence of prehospital practice rather than an indicator of individual dysfunction. Acute stress reactions occur during or immediately following an incident, with identifiable precipitant and typical resolution. Cumulative stress develops progressively over extended periods without identifiable onset, conferring greater risk owing to delayed recognition. Manifestations include sleep disturbance, irritability, social withdrawal, anhedonia, increased alcohol consumption, intrusive recollection and emotional blunting. Certain call types confer disproportionate impact irrespective of experience, including paediatric incidents, known patients, mass casualty events and incidents resembling the provider's personal circumstances. Help-seeking constitutes professional behaviour. Available support mechanisms include peer support, employee assistance programmes and professional services; familiarity with access routes prior to need is advised. Peer monitoring is appropriate, behavioural change in colleagues frequently preceding disclosure. Mandatory universal formal debriefing following significant incidents is no longer uniformly applied owing to equivocal supporting evidence, with approaches varying between services.

eli_new.analogy: Acute stress is a wave that hits you. Cumulative stress is the tide, and nobody notices the tide coming in.
eli_new.body: The reason cumulative stress is the dangerous one is that there is no moment to point at. Nothing happened. There was no call. It is a hundred ordinary shifts, and the first thing anybody notices is usually that you have stopped being yourself — and often somebody else notices before you do.

He said he was fine the first time, which is what everybody says the first time.

The second time, twenty minutes later and with nobody else around, he did not.

Nothing had happened to him. That was rather the point — nothing had happened, a hundred times, over about four years.

concepts.title: Lifting mechanics and injury prevention
key_points: Back injury ends more EMS careers than any dramatic event, and almost all of it is cumulative rather than a single moment
Keep the weight close to your body: the further out it is, the more force goes through your spine
Lift with your legs, keep your back in its natural curve, and never twist while loaded
Twisting under load is the movement most associated with injury — move your feet instead
Push rather than pull where you have the choice, and work at a height that does not require bending
Know your own limit and say so before the lift, not during it
Call for a lifting assist rather than attempting a lift you are not confident about — the delay is trivial next to a career
Use the equipment: powered stretchers, stair chairs, scoops and slide sheets exist because human backs have limits
Communicate the lift: who is in charge, what the count is, and where you are going before anybody bends down
misconceptions: Lifting from a distance because moving closer is awkward
Twisting to place a patient rather than moving the feet
Attempting a lift you are unsure about rather than waiting for help
Not agreeing who calls the lift before starting
exam_favorites: Agreeing the lift before it starts

read.plain:
More EMS careers end because of backs than because of anything dramatic. And almost none of those injuries happened in one memorable moment — it is cumulative, built out of hundreds of lifts that were each slightly wrong and none of which hurt at the time.

The mechanics are simple and they are mostly about distance. The further the weight is from your body, the more force goes through your lower spine, and it multiplies fast. The same patient held close and held at arm's length are, as far as your back is concerned, two completely different weights.

So: get close. Move yourself before you move the load, even when the furniture makes it awkward, because the awkwardness is the whole cost and the alternative is paid later.

Then the standard mechanics. Lift with your legs — they are the strongest muscles you have and they are designed for it. Keep your back in its natural curve rather than rounded. Feet apart for a stable base. Head up, because your spine follows your head.

And the single most important one: never twist while loaded. Twisting under load is the movement most associated with back injury, and it is the easiest one to do without noticing, because the patient needs to go slightly to the left and turning your shoulders is quicker than moving your feet. Move your feet. Every time.

Where you have the choice, push rather than pull — pushing lets you use your body weight and keeps the load in front of you. And set the working height so you are not bending: raise the stretcher before you work on it rather than stooping over it for twenty minutes.

Now the part that is about judgement rather than technique. Know your limit, and say so before the lift rather than during it. Saying 'I do not think I can take that corner' beforehand is a normal professional statement. Saying it halfway up a staircase is a different situation entirely.

And call for a lifting assist when you need one. Waiting eight minutes for another crew is an inconvenience. The alternative is an injury that can end the career, and nobody in the history of this job has regretted asking for help with a heavy patient down a narrow staircase.

Use the equipment. Powered stretchers, stair chairs with tracks, scoops, slide sheets, carry sheets. They exist because human backs have limits, and using them is not a sign of weakness any more than using a pen is.

Finally, talk about the lift before it happens. Who is in charge of the count. What the count actually is — 'ready, steady, lift' means different things to different people. Where the patient is going and what the route looks like. Most bad lifts go wrong because two people moved at different moments.
read.standard: Musculoskeletal injury, predominantly of the lumbar spine, constitutes the leading cause of career termination in emergency medical services, and is typically cumulative rather than resulting from single events. Biomechanical load on the lumbar spine increases substantially with distance of the load from the body, rendering proximity the primary control measure. Technique comprises lifting with the lower limbs, maintaining lumbar lordosis, a stable base of support, and neutral head position. Axial rotation under load is the movement most strongly associated with injury and is avoided by repositioning the feet. Pushing is preferred to pulling where practicable, and working height is adjusted to avoid sustained flexion. Providers should establish and communicate individual limitations prior to lifting rather than during it, and request lifting assistance where capability is uncertain; the operational delay is disproportionately small relative to injury consequence. Mechanical aids including powered stretchers, stair chairs, scoop stretchers and slide sheets are used as designed. Lifts are briefed before commencement, establishing command, the specific count, destination and route, as asynchronous movement is a principal cause of failed lifts.

eli_new.analogy: The same patient held against your chest and held at arm's length are two different weights, and only one of them is the one you think you are lifting.
eli_new.body: The movement that does the damage is not the heavy lift. It is the small twist at the end, when the patient needs to go six inches to the left and turning your shoulders is quicker than shuffling your feet. Move your feet. It is the whole technique in three words.

He had done that several thousand times over eleven years. This was the one where something gave.

concepts.title: Sleep, nutrition and fitness for duty
key_points: Fatigue degrades judgement, reaction time and mood in ways that feel exactly like being fine
Shift work disrupts the body clock, and night shifts are physiologically harder regardless of how used to them you are
Sleep debt accumulates and is not repaid by one long lie-in
Strategic napping, protecting sleep in daylight, and managing caffeine timing all help; caffeine late in a shift costs the sleep afterwards
Driving home after a night shift is one of the highest-risk things you will do all week
Eating well on shift is genuinely hard and matters: blood sugar swings affect concentration and mood
Physical fitness reduces injury risk and is part of being fit for duty, not a hobby
Fitness for duty also covers illness, medication that affects alertness, and personal circumstances that make you unsafe today
Recognising you are not fit for a shift, and saying so, is a professional act
misconceptions: Believing you have adapted to nights so they cost you nothing
Treating the drive home as the safe part of the shift
Assuming one long sleep clears accumulated debt
Working a shift you know you are not fit for
exam_favorites: Why fatigue feels like being fine
Fitness for duty as a professional judgement

read.plain:
Fatigue is dangerous in a particular way: it degrades your judgement and your reaction time while leaving your confidence completely intact. A tired clinician does not feel like an impaired clinician. They feel like themselves, making decisions that seem perfectly reasonable at the time.

Shift work fights your body clock, and night shifts are physiologically harder than day shifts no matter how many you have done. People say they have adapted. What they have usually adapted to is functioning while tired, which is not the same as not being tired.

Sleep debt accumulates. Four short nights do not get cancelled by one long lie-in, and the deficit carries forward. This is worth knowing because the natural assumption is that a good sleep resets things, and it mostly does not.

Some practical things do help. Napping strategically where your service allows it, even briefly. Protecting daytime sleep properly — blackout, phone off, household warned, because sleeping in daylight is harder and needs more defending than sleeping at night. And watching when you take caffeine: it works, and caffeine in the last part of a shift is borrowed from the sleep you are about to try to have.

The drive home after a night shift deserves singling out, because it is genuinely one of the highest-risk things you will do all week and it does not feel like it. You are at your lowest alertness, in a familiar car, on a familiar route, at a time of day when the body most wants to sleep. Plenty of EMS people have survived their whole careers and been badly hurt on the way home from them. If you are too tired, do not drive — sleep first, or get a lift.

Eating on shift is harder than it sounds and it matters more than people credit. Meals are interrupted, food is whatever is available at three in the morning, and blood sugar swinging around affects concentration, patience and mood. Carrying something reasonable with you is a small habit that pays.

Physical fitness belongs here too. It reduces injury risk directly, and it is part of being fit for duty rather than a private hobby — this job asks your body to lift, carry, kneel and climb stairs at speed.

And fitness for duty means more than fatigue. It covers being ill, being on medication that affects alertness, and personal circumstances that mean you are not safe to work today — grief, crisis, the aftermath of something. Recognising that and saying so is a professional act, not a failing. Working a shift you know you are not fit for puts a patient in the hands of somebody who has already noticed they should not be there.

Sleep debt accumulates across consecutive shifts and is not fully recovered by single extended sleep periods. Mitigation includes strategic napping where policy permits, protection of daytime sleep through environmental control, and management of caffeine timing, late-shift consumption impairing subsequent sleep. The post-night-shift commute represents a period of substantially elevated risk owing to circadian nadir, route familiarity and accumulated deficit. Nutritional management on shift affects concentration and affect through glycaemic variability. Physical conditioning reduces musculoskeletal injury risk and constitutes a component of fitness for duty. Fitness for duty additionally encompasses acute illness, medications affecting alertness, and personal circumstances compromising safe performance; self-identification and disclosure constitute professional conduct.

eli_new.analogy: Fatigue does not feel like impairment. It feels like being yourself, making reasonable decisions, in a fog you cannot see because you are inside it.
eli_new.body: The drive home is the bit nobody takes seriously. You have survived a night of genuinely dangerous work and the thing most likely to hurt you is twenty minutes on a familiar road with the sun coming up. If you are too tired, sleep in the car park. It is a completely normal thing to do.

concepts.title: Scope of practice and standard of care
key_points: Scope of practice is what you are permitted to do; standard of care is how well you must do it
Scope is set by the state and narrowed by your medical director and your service's protocols
Acting outside your scope is a legal problem even when the outcome is good
Standard of care is what a reasonable, prudent EMT with similar training would do in similar circumstances
It is not perfection and it is not hindsight — it is judged on what was reasonable with what you knew at the time
Protocols, guidelines and accepted practice all inform what the standard is
Doing less than your scope allows can breach the standard of care just as doing more breaches scope
Ethics asks what you should do; law asks what you may do, and the two usually agree but not always
misconceptions: Believing a good outcome excuses acting outside scope
Thinking standard of care means perfection
Assuming standard of care is judged with hindsight
Treating protocol as the only thing that defines the standard
exam_favorites: Doing less can also breach the standard

read.plain:
Two phrases that sound similar and mean different things.

Scope of practice is what you are permitted to do. It is set by your state, and then narrowed — by your medical director, and by your service's protocols. A skill can be in the national EMT description, absent from your state's, and that settles it. Scope is a permission list.

Standard of care is how well you must do the things you are permitted to do. It is a quality bar, not a permission list.

The standard is usually described as what a reasonable, prudent EMT with similar training would have done in similar circumstances. Three parts of that are worth noticing.

Reasonable and prudent, not perfect. The standard does not require you to be the best EMT who ever lived, or to get everything right. It requires you to act as a competent, careful person in your position would have acted.

Similar training. You are measured against EMTs, not paramedics or physicians. Not knowing something outside your training is not a breach.

Similar circumstances, judged on what you knew at the time. This is the part people worry about most and it is the part that protects them. The standard is not applied with hindsight. The question is whether your decision was reasonable given the information available then — not whether it turned out to be right.

What defines the standard, in practice: your protocols, national guidelines, accepted practice, and what your training taught you.

Now two things that are less obvious.

Acting outside your scope is a problem even when it works. If you do something you are not permitted to do and the patient does beautifully, you have still acted outside your scope. A good outcome is not a defence, and the reasoning is straightforward — the permission is not granted case by case based on results.

And doing less than your scope allows can breach the standard of care just as doing more breaches scope. Failing to do something you were trained and permitted to do, and that a reasonable EMT would have done, is a breach. This surprises people, because the instinct is that under-treating is the safe direction. It is not.

Finally, ethics and law. Law asks what you may do; ethics asks what you should. They overlap almost always. Where they diverge — a patient refusing care you are certain they need, honouring a directive you personally disagree with — you need both frameworks, and noticing that they have come apart is the skill.
read.standard: Scope of practice denotes the range of interventions a provider is authorised to perform, established by state licensure and narrowed by medical direction and service protocol. Standard of care denotes the quality with which authorised interventions must be performed, defined as the conduct of a reasonable and prudent provider of similar training in similar circumstances. The standard requires competence rather than perfection, comparison against equivalently trained providers rather than higher levels, and evaluation on information available at the time rather than retrospective knowledge. The standard is informed by protocols, national guidelines, accepted practice and training content. Practice exceeding scope constitutes a legal breach irrespective of clinical outcome, as authorisation is not conferred retrospectively by results. Failure to perform an intervention within scope that a reasonable provider would have performed constitutes a breach of the standard of care; under-treatment is not inherently protective. Legal frameworks address permissibility while ethical frameworks address obligation; divergence occurs and recognition of divergence is required.

eli_new.analogy: Scope is the list of tools you are allowed to pick up. Standard of care is how well you have to use the ones you picked.
eli_new.body: The thing that surprises people: doing less than you were allowed to can also be a breach. The instinct is that under-treating is the cautious direction and over-treating is the risky one. Both are breaches, just of different rules.

The patient improved immediately and everybody on scene could see it, which made the conversation afterwards feel unfair.

The permission to do it had never been granted, and it does not get granted retrospectively because the patient did well.

concepts.title: Consent: expressed, implied, minors and involuntary
key_points: Consent is required before touching or treating any patient, and it must be informed to be valid
Informed means the patient understands what you propose, why, the risks, and what happens if they decline
EXPRESSED consent is given directly — spoken, written, or by a clear gesture such as holding out an arm
IMPLIED consent covers a patient who cannot consent and is in an emergency: the law assumes a reasonable person would want care
Implied consent applies to the unconscious, and to those without capacity, and only for what the emergency requires
MINORS generally need a parent or guardian to consent, with exceptions for emancipated minors and for emergencies
For a minor in a genuine emergency with no guardian reachable, implied consent applies — you do not wait
INVOLUNTARY consent covers patients treated or transported under legal authority, which requires law enforcement or a designated official
Consent for one thing is not consent for everything; tell the patient what you are about to do as you go
misconceptions: Assuming a nodding patient has given informed consent
Waiting for a guardian while a child deteriorates
Treating a capacitous adult under implied consent because they seem unwise
Assuming consent to assessment means consent to transport

read.plain:
Before you touch anybody, you need their consent — and for it to count, it has to be informed.

Informed means they understand four things: what you are proposing, why you want to do it, what the risks are, and what is likely to happen if they say no. A patient who nods at you has not necessarily done any of that. Explaining properly takes about twenty seconds and it is what turns a nod into consent.

There are four types worth knowing.

Expressed consent is given directly. Spoken — 'yes, go ahead.' Written, occasionally. Or by unmistakable gesture: holding out an arm for a blood pressure cuff is expressed consent. This is what you have for almost every patient.

Implied consent covers the patient who cannot consent and is in an emergency. Unconscious, or without the capacity to decide. The law assumes that a reasonable person in that situation would want care, so you act in their best interests. It covers what the emergency requires — not everything you might like to do.

Minors generally need a parent or guardian to consent. There are exceptions: emancipated minors, who are legally treated as adults, and in many jurisdictions minors who are married, in the armed forces, or seeking care for certain specific things. Know your state's rules.

And here is the part that matters at three in the morning: for a minor in a genuine emergency with no guardian reachable, implied consent applies. You do not wait. You do not stand there while a child deteriorates because nobody has answered the phone. Treat, document what you did to reach a guardian, and keep trying.

Involuntary consent is the fourth, and it is the one that needs somebody else's authority. It covers patients treated or transported against their wishes under a legal framework — typically because they are a danger to themselves or others. That framework differs by jurisdiction and it almost never lets an EMT act alone: it needs law enforcement, a physician, or another designated official depending on your system.

One last thing that gets forgotten. Consent for one thing is not consent for everything. A patient agreeing to be assessed has not agreed to be transported. Someone who let you take a blood pressure has not agreed to a needle. Keep telling them what you are about to do as you go — it is both good practice and how consent actually stays valid through a call.
read.standard: Valid consent is required prior to assessment or treatment and must be informed, requiring patient comprehension of the proposed intervention, its rationale, associated risks and the consequences of refusal. Expressed consent is communicated directly by speech, writing or unambiguous gesture. Implied consent applies where a patient lacks capacity to consent and an emergency exists, on the legal presumption that a reasonable person would accept necessary care; it extends only to interventions the emergency requires. Minors ordinarily require parental or guardian consent, with exceptions for emancipated minors and jurisdiction-specific categories including married minors, military service members and care for specified conditions. Where a genuine emergency exists and no guardian is reachable, implied consent applies to minors and treatment proceeds without delay, with attempts at contact documented. Involuntary consent applies to patients treated or transported under statutory authority, typically for danger to self or others, and generally requires law enforcement, physician or designated official involvement rather than independent EMT action. Consent is intervention-specific; consent to assessment does not extend to transport, and ongoing explanation maintains validity.

eli_new.analogy: Consent is not a signature at the start. It is a running conversation that has to keep up with what your hands are doing.
eli_new.body: The one to be absolutely clear about: a child in a real emergency with no parent reachable gets treated. You do not stand and wait. Implied consent covers it, you document what you did to reach somebody, and you keep trying while you work.

concepts.title: Refusal of care and documentation
key_points: A competent adult may refuse care, including care that will save their life, and that right is real
Before accepting a refusal, establish capacity: can they understand, retain, weigh and communicate a decision about this
Check for anything that impairs capacity: low blood sugar, hypoxia, head injury, intoxication, infection
A refusal from somebody without capacity is not a valid refusal
The refusal must be informed — they must understand what may happen if they decline, in plain words
Try to persuade, more than once, and involve family or medical direction where it may help
Document the capacity assessment, what you told them, what they said in their own words, and who witnessed it
Leave the door open: tell them explicitly to call again if anything changes, and mean it
Refusal is the highest-risk thing an EMT does routinely, and the documentation is the whole defence
misconceptions: Accepting a refusal without assessing capacity
Not checking a glucose before accepting a refusal
Recording 'patient refused' and nothing else
Leaving without telling the patient to call back if things change
exam_favorites: Why a refusal must be informed

read.plain:
A competent adult may refuse care. All of it. Including care that would save their life, and including when everybody present thinks they are wrong. That right is real and it does not depend on you agreeing with the decision.

But every word of that sentence rests on the word competent, and that is where your work is.

Before you accept a refusal, establish capacity. Can this person understand what you are telling them? Retain it long enough to use it? Weigh it up against the alternatives? And communicate a decision? All four, about this specific decision, now.

And critically: look for anything that is impairing it. A blood glucose. An oxygen saturation. A head injury from the fall they are refusing to be assessed for. Intoxication. An infection in an older person. Any of those can take capacity away, and a refusal from somebody without capacity is not a valid refusal at all.

This is why the glucose meter comes out before the refusal form. A hypoglycaemic patient refusing transport is not making a decision; they are exhibiting a symptom.

The refusal also has to be informed, and informed means plain words. Not 'you may suffer adverse consequences.' Say what could actually happen: that they could bleed inside their head and not wake up, that the chest pain could be a heart attack and they could die at home tonight. It feels blunt. It is what informed means, and a refusal based on a gentle euphemism is not informed.

Try to persuade. More than once, and differently the second time. Involve family if the patient is willing. Call medical direction — many services require it, and a physician on the phone sometimes changes a mind that a crew could not.

Then document, because this is the part that matters most. Your capacity assessment and what you based it on. The vital signs, including the glucose. Exactly what you told them about the risks. What they said back, in their own words, in quotation marks. Who was present. Who witnessed the refusal. What you advised them to do if things change.

And leave the door open, out loud. 'If anything changes at all, or you change your mind, call us straight back — we will come, and nobody will mind.' Say it, mean it, and write down that you said it. People who have refused once are often embarrassed to call again, and that sentence is sometimes what brings them back.

Refusals are the highest-risk thing an EMT does routinely. Not the cardiac arrests — those are clear. It is the patient who looked fine, refused, and deteriorated after you left. The documentation is the entire defence, and more importantly, the process behind it is what stops it happening.
read.standard: Adults with decision-making capacity may decline care, including life-sustaining intervention, irrespective of provider or family disagreement. Capacity assessment precedes acceptance of refusal and requires that the patient understand relevant information, retain it, weigh it against alternatives and communicate a decision regarding the specific matter at hand. Assessment includes identification of capacity-impairing conditions: hypoglycaemia, hypoxia, traumatic brain injury, intoxication and infection. Refusal by a patient lacking capacity is invalid. Blood glucose and oxygen saturation measurement precede acceptance of refusal. Informed refusal requires explanation of consequences in plain language with specific reference to realistic outcomes rather than euphemism. Persuasion should be attempted repeatedly and by varied approach, with involvement of family and medical direction where appropriate; many services mandate physician consultation. Documentation records the capacity assessment and its basis, vital signs including glucose, information provided, patient statements verbatim, persons present, witnesses, and advice given regarding re-contact. Patients are explicitly advised to re-contact services if circumstances change or they reconsider. Refusals constitute the highest-frequency high-risk encounter in prehospital practice.

eli_new.analogy: A refusal is a decision, and a decision needs a decider. Your job before accepting one is establishing that there is somebody in there capable of making it.
eli_new.body: The glucose meter comes out before the refusal form. A patient with a sugar of 2.5 refusing transport is not making a decision — they are showing you a symptom, and accepting it as a refusal is accepting a symptom as a choice.

Somebody checked a glucose first, because that is the habit, and it was 2.5.

Twenty minutes later he consented to everything and could not remember refusing anything. The refusal had never been a decision.

concepts.title: Negligence: the four elements, and abandonment
key_points: Negligence requires ALL FOUR elements to be present — if any one is missing, there is no negligence
DUTY: you had an obligation to act, which on duty and dispatched to a patient you do
BREACH (dereliction): you failed to meet the standard of care — by doing something wrong or by failing to do something
CAUSATION: the breach actually caused harm, directly rather than coincidentally
DAMAGES: real harm resulted — physical, psychological or financial
Causation is where many claims fail: a mistake that harmed nobody is a mistake, not negligence
Abandonment is ending care without the patient's consent and without handing over to someone of equal or higher training
Abandonment can happen at the hospital as easily as on scene — leaving a patient on a corridor trolley without handing over is abandonment
Once you start care you have accepted a duty, and it continues until it is properly transferred
misconceptions: Believing a single error automatically means negligence
Thinking abandonment only happens on scene
Handing over to a receptionist or a porter
Leaving a patient in a waiting area without a handover to clinical staff
exam_favorites: The four elements and that all four are required

read.plain:
Negligence is a legal finding, and it has four elements. All four have to be present. If any single one is missing, there is no negligence — which is worth holding onto, because the word gets used loosely and frightens people more than it should.

Duty. You had an obligation to act. On duty and dispatched to a patient, you do. Off duty in another state at a road crash, the position is different and depends on your jurisdiction.

Breach — sometimes called dereliction. You failed to meet the standard of care. That can be doing something wrong, or failing to do something a reasonable EMT would have done. Both directions count.

Causation. The breach actually caused the harm. Directly — not coincidentally, not 'happened on the same call as'.

Damages. Real harm resulted: physical, psychological or financial.

Causation is where a great many claims fail, and understanding why is genuinely reassuring. A mistake that harmed nobody is a mistake. It is worth reporting, worth learning from, and it is not negligence, because the third and fourth elements are missing. Equally, a patient who did badly after a call where everything was done correctly has damages but no breach.

The four elements are conventionally taught as the four Ds: Duty, Dereliction, Direct cause, Damages.

Abandonment is separate and specific. It is ending care without the patient's consent and without transferring them to somebody of equal or higher training.

Two things about it surprise people.

First, it can happen at the hospital just as easily as on scene — and more often does. You wheel a patient into a busy department, there is nowhere to put them, nobody is free, you are being called for another job, and you leave them on a trolley in a corridor without handing over to a nurse. That is abandonment. The building is full of clinicians, and none of them has accepted this patient from you. Handing over to a receptionist or a porter is not a handover.

Second, once you begin care you have accepted a duty, and it continues until it is properly transferred. You cannot start and then decide this patient was not really yours.

The practical version: find a person of equal or greater training, tell them about the patient, make sure they have accepted, and write down who and when.
read.standard: Negligence requires the concurrent presence of four elements; absence of any one negates the finding. Duty denotes an obligation to act, present when on duty and dispatched; off-duty obligation varies by jurisdiction. Breach, or dereliction, denotes failure to meet the standard of care, by commission or omission. Causation requires that the breach directly produced the harm rather than being temporally coincident. Damages require actual harm, physical, psychological or financial. Causation and damages are frequently absent: error without resultant harm does not constitute negligence, and adverse outcome following appropriate care establishes damages without breach. The elements are conventionally taught as the four Ds: Duty, Dereliction, Direct cause, Damages. Abandonment denotes termination of care without patient consent and without transfer to a provider of equal or greater training. It occurs in hospital settings as readily as prehospital, including leaving patients in corridors or waiting areas without clinical handover; transfer to non-clinical staff does not constitute handover. Duty commences with initiation of care and persists until formal transfer, which should be documented with recipient identity and time.

eli_new.analogy: Negligence is a four-legged stool. Remove any leg and it is not a stool any more — it is just some wood.
eli_new.body: The one that catches crews out is abandonment at hospital. A full department, nowhere to put the patient, another job waiting, and you leave them on a trolley in a corridor. The building is full of clinicians and not one of them has accepted this patient from you. Find a nurse, hand over, get a name.

Breach can be doing something wrong or failing to do something
Causation is where many claims fail — a mistake that harmed nobody is not negligence
Abandonment is ending care without consent and without handing over to equal or higher training
