The department was full, there was genuinely nowhere to put her, and the crew had another call holding.

They left her on a trolley in a corridor in a building full of doctors and nurses.

Not one of whom had accepted her from them, which is what makes it abandonment rather than a busy shift.

expansion: D — DUTY: you had an obligation to act. On duty and dispatched, you do. Off duty depends on your jurisdiction.
D — DERELICTION: you breached the standard of care — by doing something wrong, OR by failing to do something a reasonable EMT would have done.
D — DIRECT CAUSE: the breach actually caused the harm. Directly, not coincidentally. This is where many claims fail.
D — DAMAGES: real harm resulted — physical, psychological or financial.
ALL FOUR OR NONE. A mistake that harmed nobody has no cause and no damages; a bad outcome after correct care has damages but no breach.

concepts.title: Confidentiality and health information privacy
key_points: Patient information is confidential and may only be shared where there is a legitimate need to know
Legitimate sharing includes clinical handover, your own documentation, quality improvement, and legally required reporting
Family and friends are not automatically entitled to information, even when they are helping and mean well
The commonest real breaches are casual: discussing a call in a corridor, a public place, or on social media
Never post about a call, anywhere, even without a name — details identify people far more easily than posters expect
Photographs of patients, scenes or injuries on a personal phone are a breach
Leaving a report visible on a screen or a clipboard is a breach of the same kind as talking about it
Breaches carry disciplinary, professional and legal consequences, and this is one of the commonest ways EMS careers end
misconceptions: Telling a relative details because they seem entitled
Discussing a call in a hospital lift or a public corridor
Posting a 'no names' account on social media
Photographing an interesting injury
exam_favorites: Who counts as a need to know

read.plain:
Everything you learn about a patient is confidential. Their condition, their history, their address, the state of their house, who was there, what they said. All of it.

You may share it where there is a legitimate need to know. That covers clinical handover to the people taking over care, your own documentation, quality improvement review, and reporting that the law requires — safeguarding, certain communicable diseases, some injuries.

It does not automatically cover family and friends. This feels harsh, because the daughter asking what is wrong with her mother is worried and helpful and standing right there. But she is not automatically entitled to clinical information, and the decision is generally the patient's rather than yours. Where the patient can express a preference, ask them.

Now the part worth being blunt about: the breaches that actually happen are not dramatic. Almost nobody sells records. What happens is ordinary and careless.

Discussing a call in a hospital corridor, in a lift, in a queue, in a canteen. You are talking to a colleague about clinical detail and the person behind you knows the patient. Hospitals and towns are much smaller than they feel.

Social media, which is where careers end. A post about an interesting call, no name used, perhaps no location. It is not enough. A date, a rough age, a mechanism and a town identify a person to anybody who knows them, and it takes one relative recognising the story. The rule is simple: do not post about calls. Not with names removed, not in a private group, not years later.

Photographs on a personal phone are a breach whether or not you show anybody. An interesting injury, an unusual scene, a striking ECG — if it is on your phone it should not be. Where clinical images are genuinely needed there is a service process for it; use that.

And screens and paperwork. A report left visible on a monitor, a clipboard on a counter, a handover sheet in a bin rather than confidential waste. Same category of breach as talking about it, and easier to do without noticing.

Consequences are real: disciplinary, professional registration, and legal. This is genuinely one of the commonest ways EMS careers end — not through a clinical error on a difficult call, but through a post, a photograph, or a conversation in the wrong place.
read.standard: Patient information is confidential and disclosed only where a legitimate need to know exists, comprising clinical handover, documentation, quality improvement activity and legally mandated reporting including safeguarding, notifiable disease and specified injury categories. Family members and associates hold no automatic entitlement to clinical information; disclosure decisions generally rest with the patient where capacity permits and preference should be elicited. The predominant source of actual breach is inadvertent rather than deliberate: clinical discussion in public areas, corridors, lifts and communal spaces, where third-party recognition of the patient is more probable than providers assume. Social media disclosure constitutes breach irrespective of name omission, as date, approximate age, mechanism and location permit identification. Photography of patients, scenes or injuries on personal devices constitutes breach irrespective of onward disclosure; clinical imaging requirements are addressed through service process. Unattended visible documentation, whether electronic or paper, constitutes breach of equivalent category. Consequences include disciplinary action, professional registration sanction and legal liability; confidentiality breach is among the most frequent causes of EMS career termination.

eli_new.analogy: De-identifying a story is much harder than it feels. A date, an age and a mechanism is a name to anybody who already knows the person.
eli_new.body: The one that ends careers is social media. Not the obvious version with a name on it — the careful version, with the name removed, posted because the call was remarkable. It takes one relative recognising the details, and they do.

concepts.title: Advance directives, DNR and POLST
key_points: An advance directive records what a patient wants if they cannot speak for themselves
A DNR order says do not attempt resuscitation if the heart or breathing stops — it does not say do not treat
This is the single most important point: a DNR patient still gets pain relief, oxygen, positioning, comfort and dignity
A POLST or similar physician order form is more detailed, covering several interventions rather than resuscitation alone
The document has to be valid and available — requirements differ by jurisdiction and your protocol will specify what counts
If there is genuine doubt about validity, or the document cannot be found, begin resuscitation — you can stop, and you cannot undo not starting
Family distress does not override a valid directive, and family insistence does not create one
Where family conflict arises, contact medical direction rather than deciding alone
Document what you saw, who was present, and what you did
misconceptions: Treating a DNR as do not treat

What to do when the document is missing or unclear

read.plain:
An advance directive is a patient speaking in advance about what they want if they reach a point where they cannot say.

A do-not-resuscitate order is one kind. It says that if the heart stops or breathing stops, no attempt at resuscitation should be made.

And here is the point that matters more than anything else in this concept, because it gets misunderstood constantly: a DNR is not do not treat.

A patient with a valid DNR still gets everything else. Pain relief within your scope. Oxygen if they are short of breath. Suction. Positioning. Warmth. Being talked to. Being transported if that is what they need. Having their family supported. A DNR speaks to one specific moment — cardiac or respiratory arrest — and says nothing whatsoever about the care before it.

Patients with DNR orders have been left uncomfortable and under-treated by crews who read those three letters and stopped thinking. That is a failure of care, not a respecting of wishes.

A POLST — or whatever equivalent your jurisdiction uses — goes further. It is a physician's order covering several decisions: resuscitation, yes, but also intubation, hospitalisation, antibiotics, artificial feeding. It is usually more useful to you than a DNR alone because it says more.

For any of it to apply, the document has to be valid and it has to be available. What counts as valid differs by jurisdiction — original versus copy, specific forms, bracelets, registry entries, signatures and dates. Your protocol will specify. Learn it before you are kneeling on a bedroom floor at four in the morning trying to read a form.

And the rule for when it is not clear: if there is genuine doubt about validity, or the document cannot be found, begin resuscitation. The reasoning is asymmetric. You can stop once a valid document appears. You cannot undo not starting. Somebody saying there is a DNR somewhere in the house is not a document.

Family distress does not override a valid directive. A daughter saying 'do something' in the moment does not cancel her father's written wishes, and this is one of the harder things you will do. Equally, family insistence does not create a directive where there is no document.

When family conflict arises — and it does — contact medical direction rather than deciding alone. That is what it is for.

And document: what document you saw, whether it appeared valid, who was present, what they said, and what you did.
read.standard: Advance directives record patient preferences for circumstances in which they cannot communicate. Do-not-resuscitate orders direct that resuscitation not be attempted following cardiac or respiratory arrest; they do not restrict other treatment. Patients with valid DNR orders receive analgesia within scope, oxygen, suction, positioning, warming, communication, transport as indicated and family support; under-treatment of DNR patients constitutes a failure of care rather than respect for expressed wishes. POLST and equivalent physician order forms address multiple interventions including resuscitation, intubation, hospitalisation, antimicrobial therapy and artificial nutrition, providing greater operational guidance. Application requires document validity and availability; validity criteria including original versus copy, prescribed forms, identification bracelets and registry entries vary by jurisdiction and are specified by protocol. Where validity is genuinely doubtful or documentation is unavailable, resuscitation is commenced, as cessation remains possible following document production whereas non-initiation is irreversible; verbal report of an existing directive does not constitute documentation. Family distress does not invalidate a valid directive and family assertion does not create one. Familial conflict warrants medical direction consultation. Documentation records the document observed, apparent validity, persons present, statements made and actions taken.

eli_new.analogy: A DNR is a note about one moment — the moment the heart stops. It says nothing about the hours before it, and those hours are still yours to make bearable.
eli_new.body: If you take one thing: a DNR patient gets pain relief, oxygen, comfort and dignity. Those three letters mean do not attempt resuscitation. They have never meant do not care for this person, and reading them that way is how patients get left uncomfortable by well-meaning crews.

concepts.title: Mandatory reporting and crime scene preservation
key_points: Some things must be reported by law regardless of the patient's wishes, and the categories vary by jurisdiction
Commonly mandated: suspected child abuse or neglect, suspected elder or vulnerable adult abuse, certain injuries such as gunshot and stab wounds, and specified communicable diseases
Mandatory reporting requires suspicion, not proof — you are not investigating and you do not need to be sure
Report through the route your service specifies, and document that you did
At a crime scene, patient care comes first — nothing about evidence outweighs a living patient
Disturb as little as possible while doing what the patient needs: take one route in and out, and touch only what you must
Do not cut through clothing holes made by a bullet or blade; cut around them
Keep removed clothing, place it in paper rather than plastic where policy directs, and hand it to police
Record what you moved, what you touched and why, and tell the investigating officer
misconceptions: Waiting for proof before reporting a suspicion
Delaying care to preserve a scene
Cutting through a bullet hole in clothing
Putting bloodstained clothing into a plastic bag
exam_favorites: Cutting around defects, not through them

read.plain:
Some things you must report by law, whatever the patient wants and whatever you would prefer. What falls in that category depends on where you work, so learn your list — but the common ones are consistent.

Suspected child abuse or neglect. Suspected abuse of an elder or vulnerable adult. Certain injuries — gunshot wounds, stab wounds, and in some places burns or injuries from particular causes. Specified communicable diseases. Some jurisdictions add animal bites, or suspected drug-endangered children, or others.

The key word is suspicion. You do not need proof, you do not need to be sure, and you are absolutely not investigating. Your obligation is to report what you observed and what concerned you. Somebody else determines what it means. Waiting until you are certain is how things go unreported for years, and being wrong about a suspicion has no consequence for you — the system exists to sort that out.

Report through your service's route and document that you did it, including who you reported to and when.

Crime scenes are the other half of this. And the first principle is the one that outranks everything: patient care comes first. No piece of evidence is worth more than a living patient, and nobody has ever been criticised for disturbing a scene in order to treat somebody. If you have to move furniture, walk through something, or cut across a room to reach a patient, do it.

Within that, disturb as little as you can manage.

Take one route in and use the same route out. Touch only what you need to. Do not tidy, do not pick things up to look at them, and do not let bystanders or family move things if you can help it.

One specific thing that catches people: do not cut through a hole in clothing made by a bullet or a blade. That hole is evidence — its shape and its edges tell an examiner things. Cut around it. It takes no longer.

Keep the clothing you remove. Bag it, using paper rather than plastic where your policy says so — plastic traps moisture and degrades biological evidence — and hand it to police rather than leaving it in a corner or a hospital bin.

And tell the investigating officer what you did. What you moved, what you touched, what you cut, where you walked, who else was there when you arrived. They are not going to be annoyed that you disturbed things to treat somebody. They will be considerably more annoyed if nobody tells them what was moved and they spend two days working it out.
read.standard: Statutory reporting obligations exist irrespective of patient preference, with mandated categories varying by jurisdiction. Commonly mandated categories include suspected child abuse and neglect, suspected elder and vulnerable adult abuse, specified injuries including gunshot and stab wounds, and notifiable communicable diseases. The threshold is reasonable suspicion rather than proof; providers are not investigators and are not required to establish certainty. Reporting follows service-specified process with documentation of the report, recipient and time. At crime scenes, patient care takes absolute precedence over evidence preservation. Scene disturbance is minimised within that constraint: a single route of entry and egress, minimal contact, avoidance of tidying or repositioning, and discouragement of bystander interference. Clothing defects produced by projectiles or blades are not incised through, as defect morphology carries forensic value; cutting is performed around such defects. Removed clothing is retained, packaged in paper rather than plastic where policy directs owing to moisture retention and biological degradation, and transferred to law enforcement. Providers report to investigating officers what was moved, contacted, incised, the route taken and persons present on arrival.

eli_new.analogy: You are not preserving a scene. You are treating a patient in a room that happens to matter to somebody else, and then telling them what you had to change.
eli_new.body: Two practical things that cost nothing. Cut around the hole in the shirt rather than through it. And tell the officer what you moved — they will not mind that you moved it, and they will mind a great deal if nobody says.

The threshold is suspicion, not proof — you are not investigating
Patient care comes before evidence

story.title: Round the hole
story.dispatch: Medic 5 — penetrating chest wound, police on scene.
story.body:
Exposing the chest took four seconds and the shears went round the defect in the shirt rather than through it, which took no longer.

At the end, the EMT told the officer which door they had used, what they had moved, and that the shirt was in a paper bag.

He said it was the most useful thing anybody had said to him all night.

concepts.title: Good Samaritan laws and immunity
key_points: Good Samaritan laws are intended to protect people who help voluntarily, in good faith, without expectation of payment
They generally require that you acted in good faith, within your training, and without gross negligence or wilful misconduct
They do not protect you from acting recklessly, and they do not protect acts far outside your training
Whether they apply to on-duty providers varies by jurisdiction — in many places they do not, because you already have a duty to act
Off duty, whether you have a duty to act at all also varies: some jurisdictions impose one on licensed providers, most do not
Once you begin helping, you have generally assumed a duty and cannot simply walk away
Immunity provisions and their limits differ substantially between states, and general descriptions are not a substitute for knowing yours
Acting within your training, doing what a reasonable person at your level would do, and not abandoning is the practical protection
misconceptions: Assuming Good Samaritan protection covers on-duty work
Believing it protects any action taken with good intentions
Starting to help and then leaving when it becomes inconvenient
Assuming there is always a duty to act off duty

read.plain:
Good Samaritan laws exist to remove a disincentive. Without them, somebody who stopped to help at a road crash might reasonably fear being sued for it, and the result would be fewer people stopping. So the law offers protection.

The protection generally requires three things. You acted in good faith — genuinely trying to help. You acted without expectation of payment. And you acted within your training and without gross negligence or wilful misconduct.

That last clause is the one that matters. Good Samaritan protection does not cover recklessness. It does not cover doing something wildly outside your training because it seemed like a good idea. It covers a reasonable person, acting reasonably, who got something wrong — which is the situation it was written for.

Now two questions where the honest answer is that it depends on where you are.

Does it apply to you on duty? In many jurisdictions, no. The reasoning is that Good Samaritan protection exists for volunteers, and on duty you already have a duty to act and are covered by other arrangements — your service's insurance, your medical director. So do not think of it as a general shield over your working life. It is not.

Do you have a duty to act off duty? Also varies. Some jurisdictions impose a duty on licensed providers even off duty. Most do not, leaving it an ethical question rather than a legal one. Know which yours is, because it genuinely changes what you are obliged to do when you drive past something.

One thing is consistent almost everywhere, and it is the important one: once you begin helping, you have generally assumed a duty. You cannot start, decide it is more than you expected, and walk away. That is abandonment in most frameworks, and it applies to the off-duty roadside just as it does on shift.

So the practical position: the specifics differ substantially between states, and a general description like this one is not a substitute for knowing yours. What protects you in practice is acting within your training, doing what a reasonable person at your level would do in the circumstances, and not leaving somebody you have started helping.
read.standard: Good Samaritan statutes provide liability protection for voluntary assistance rendered in good faith without expectation of remuneration, generally conditional on action within the provider's training and absence of gross negligence or wilful misconduct. Protection does not extend to reckless conduct or intervention substantially exceeding training. Applicability to on-duty providers varies by jurisdiction and is frequently excluded, as on-duty personnel bear an existing duty to act and are covered by employer indemnity and medical direction arrangements. Off-duty duty to act likewise varies: certain jurisdictions impose a duty on licensed providers, while most treat the matter as ethical rather than statutory. Initiation of assistance generally establishes an assumed duty precluding subsequent withdrawal, constituting abandonment in most frameworks and applying equally to off-duty circumstances. Statutory provisions and their limitations differ substantially between jurisdictions; general descriptions do not substitute for knowledge of applicable local law. Practical protection derives from acting within training, conformity to reasonable conduct at the provider's level, and non-abandonment.

eli_new.analogy: Good Samaritan law is a shield for the person who stopped, not a licence for the person who improvised.
eli_new.body: The most consistent and most practical part: once you start helping, you have taken it on. You cannot begin at a roadside, realise it is worse than you thought, and get back in your car. That applies off duty just as much as on shift.

It requires acting within training and without gross negligence
It does not protect reckless acts or acts far outside training
Whether it applies on duty varies and frequently does not
Whether there is a duty to act off duty varies by jurisdiction
Once you begin helping you generally assume a duty and cannot walk away

story.title: Back in the car
story.dispatch: Off duty — roadside collision, one EMT stopped, then left before help arrived.
story.body:
He stopped because he was the only one there, started a primary assessment, and found it was considerably worse than it had looked from the road.

He went back to his car and drove on, and an ambulance arrived eleven minutes later.

Not stopping at all would have been a question about duty. Starting and then leaving is a different question entirely.

concepts.title: Radio systems and etiquette
key_points: Simplex radios transmit and receive on one frequency, so only one person can speak at a time
Duplex systems use two frequencies and allow both parties to speak at once, like a telephone
A repeater receives a weak signal and rebroadcasts it at higher power, which is how portable radios reach far away
Press the transmit button, pause briefly, then speak — the first half-second of speech is routinely cut off
Speak across the microphone rather than into it, at a normal pace and volume, and keep it a consistent distance away
Be brief, be clear, and think about what you are going to say before you press the button
Use plain language: many systems have moved away from codes because they are inconsistent between agencies
Never use a patient's name on the radio, and never say anything you would not want broadcast — because it is
Acknowledge that you received a message, and ask for a repeat rather than guessing
misconceptions: Speaking immediately on pressing transmit
Shouting into a radio when the signal is poor
Using agency-specific codes with an agency that does not share them
Saying a patient's name over the air
exam_favorites: Why the first half-second is lost

read.plain:
A few pieces of vocabulary, then the part that actually matters.

Simplex means one frequency: transmit and receive on the same channel, so only one person can speak at a time. Push to talk, release to listen. Most portable radio traffic works this way, which is why talking over each other loses both messages.

Duplex uses two frequencies, so both parties can speak and hear at once, like a telephone. Some hospital notification systems work this way.

A repeater sits somewhere high, receives a weak signal from a handheld radio, and rebroadcasts it at much higher power. It is why a small radio in a basement can reach a control room forty miles away — and why, when you are out of repeater range, that same radio suddenly cannot reach anybody.

Now the practical habits, which matter more than the theory.

Press the button, pause for about half a second, then speak. Radios take a moment to open the channel, and the first fraction of what you say is routinely lost. Everybody who has ever said 'Medic 4' and heard 'say again' knows this without knowing why.

Hold the microphone a consistent distance away and speak across it rather than directly into it, which reduces popping. Normal pace, normal volume. Shouting into a radio when the signal is poor makes you less intelligible, not more — the problem is the signal, not your volume.

Think before you press. The most common radio failure is not technical; it is somebody transmitting while still working out what they want to say. Compose it first, then key up.

Use plain language. Many systems have moved away from numeric codes, because a code that means one thing in your agency means something else in the one next door, and mutual aid incidents are exactly where that matters. Say what you mean.

And two things never to do. Do not use a patient's name over the air. And do not say anything you would not want broadcast — because it is being broadcast, and scanners exist, and recordings are kept.

Finally, acknowledge what you receive so the other party knows it arrived, and ask for a repeat rather than guessing. Guessing at a half-heard address costs far more time than asking.
read.standard: Simplex radio systems transmit and receive on a single frequency, permitting unidirectional communication at any moment. Duplex systems employ paired frequencies enabling simultaneous bidirectional communication. Repeaters receive low-power transmissions and rebroadcast at higher power from elevated positions, extending portable radio range; coverage ceases beyond repeater range. Operational technique requires a brief pause following key activation before speech, as initial transmission is routinely truncated during channel establishment. The microphone is held at consistent distance with speech directed across rather than into it, at normal rate and volume; increased volume does not improve intelligibility where signal quality is the limiting factor. Message composition precedes transmission. Plain language is preferred to numeric codes, which vary between agencies and create ambiguity during mutual aid operations. Patient identifiers are not transmitted. All transmissions are presumed public and recorded. Receipt is acknowledged and clarification requested rather than assumed.

eli_new.analogy: A radio is a corridor one person can walk down at a time. Two people setting off at once means nobody gets through.
eli_new.body: Press, wait half a second, then talk. That one habit fixes most of the 'say again' traffic you will ever hear, and almost nobody is taught why it happens.

story.title: Say again
story.dispatch: Control — four transmissions, three of them repeated.
story.body:
Every one began with a unit number that nobody heard, because the speaking started at the same instant as the button.

The fourth crew pressed, counted one, and then spoke.

Control got it first time, which is roughly thirty seconds saved across four messages and considerably more across a shift.

concepts.title: The radio report and hospital notification
key_points: The radio report tells the hospital what is coming so they can prepare, and it is not a full handover
Keep it short: unit, level of care, age and sex, chief complaint, brief history, vital signs, treatment given, and estimated arrival
Lead with what changes what they do — a critical patient, a stroke alert, a trauma activation, a cardiac arrest
Say the trigger word if there is one: sepsis, stroke, STEMI, major trauma — those words mobilise a team
Give an honest estimated time of arrival, and update it if it changes substantially
Do not editorialise, speculate on diagnosis beyond your scope, or use a patient's name
Ask for what you need: a resuscitation room, a paramedic intercept, a specific specialty
Confirm the hospital received and understood, and note the name of who you spoke to
misconceptions: Giving a full narrative on the radio
Burying the critical detail at the end
Not using the trigger word because it feels dramatic
Giving an unrealistic arrival time
exam_favorites: Leading with what changes their actions

read.plain:
The radio report is not a handover. It is a heads-up, and its only job is to let the hospital prepare before you get there.

That purpose decides its shape. Everything in it should be something that changes what they do in the next few minutes. Everything else waits until you are standing in front of them.

A workable order: who you are and what level of care. Age and sex. The chief complaint. A brief relevant history. Vital signs. What you have done. Estimated time of arrival. Anything you need on arrival.

But the order matters less than one principle: lead with what changes their actions. If this is a critical patient, say so in the first sentence. A hospital that discovers on sentence six that you are bringing a cardiac arrest has lost five sentences of preparation.

Which brings us to trigger words, and these are worth taking seriously. Sepsis. Stroke. STEMI. Major trauma. Cardiac arrest. In most systems those words activate a specific pathway — a team is pulled together, a scanner is cleared, a theatre is warned. Saying 'query sepsis' does something that 'unwell elderly patient' does not, and the difference is measured in people already waiting when your doors open.

Say the word if it applies. It can feel dramatic, particularly when you are not certain. That hesitancy costs patients time, and a stood-down alert costs a hospital almost nothing.

Give an honest arrival time. Guessing short to sound efficient means a team standing waiting; guessing long means they are not ready. And update it if it changes significantly.

A few things to leave out. Do not editorialise — the radio is not the place for your view of the family or the scene. Do not offer a diagnosis beyond your scope; describe findings and let them interpret. And no names.

Ask for what you need. A resuscitation room. A paramedic intercept en route. A specific specialty team standing by. They cannot arrange what you did not ask for.

And confirm it landed — that they received it and understood it, and who you spoke to. A report nobody acted on is the same as a report nobody made.
read.standard: The prearrival radio report provides advance notification to enable facility preparation and does not constitute formal handover. Content comprises unit identification and level of care, patient age and sex, chief complaint, pertinent history, vital signs, interventions performed, estimated time of arrival and specific requirements on arrival. Information is prioritised by its effect on receiving facility action, with critical status communicated in the opening sentence. Institutional trigger terminology — sepsis, stroke, ST-elevation myocardial infarction, major trauma, cardiac arrest — activates predetermined pathways mobilising personnel and resources, and should be used where criteria are met despite diagnostic uncertainty; deactivation of an alert carries minimal institutional cost relative to delayed activation. Estimated arrival times are stated accurately and updated on material change. Editorial comment, diagnostic speculation beyond scope and patient identifiers are excluded. Specific resource requests are made explicitly. Receipt and comprehension are confirmed with documentation of the recipient.

eli_new.analogy: A radio report is a telegram, not a letter. Everything in it should earn its place by changing what somebody does before you arrive.
eli_new.body: Say the trigger word. It feels dramatic when you are not certain, and a stood-down alert costs a hospital almost nothing while a late one costs a patient a great deal.

Lead with what changes their actions

story.dispatch: Hospital feedback — pre-alert for a cardiac arrest.

The report was thorough and well organised and gave the history in careful order.

The word arrest appeared about forty seconds in.

The team that would have been assembled in those forty seconds was instead assembled afterwards, which is the same team arriving later.

concepts.title: Verbal handover at the bedside
key_points: Handover is the moment care transfers, and most information lost in a patient's journey is lost here
Use a structure so nothing is dropped — SBAR and MIST are two common ones and your service may specify
SBAR: Situation, Background, Assessment, Recommendation
MIST: Mechanism, Injuries, Signs, Treatment — commonly used for trauma
Get the receiving clinician's attention first and make sure they are actually listening before you start
Give it once, to the person taking over, rather than in fragments to whoever is passing
Include what you found that they cannot see: the scene, the position you found them in, what the family said, what the house looked like
Say what has changed during your care, not only the current state
Handover is not complete until somebody has accepted the patient, and you should know their name
misconceptions: Starting a handover before the receiving clinician is listening
Giving fragments to several different people
Reporting only current observations and omitting the trend
Leaving before anybody has accepted the patient

read.plain:
Handover is the point at which care transfers from you to somebody else, and more information is lost at handovers than anywhere else in a patient's journey through the system. Not in assessment, not in treatment — in the transfer.

So use a structure. It stops you dropping things when you are tired or when the department is loud.

SBAR is one: Situation — who this is and what is wrong now. Background — the relevant history. Assessment — what you found, including vital signs. Recommendation — what you think they need.

MIST is another, used commonly for trauma: Mechanism — what happened. Injuries — what you found. Signs — vital signs and their trend. Treatment — what you did and how they responded.

Your service may specify one; if it does, use it, because a structure everybody shares is worth more than a better structure only you use.

Before any of it: get the receiving clinician's attention and check they are actually listening. Handing over to somebody typing, or to the back of a head, is not handing over. A short 'are you ready for this one?' and waiting for an answer is worth the four seconds.

Give it once, to the person taking over. Not in fragments to whoever passes — that produces four people with a quarter each and nobody with the whole picture.

And here is the part with the most value in it: include what you found that they cannot see. They will get the vital signs from the monitor and the injuries from examining. What they can never get is the scene. That she was found on the floor and had been there since yesterday. That there were eleven empty packets by the chair. That the house was freezing. That her son said she has not been herself for a week. That is information that exists nowhere except in your head, and once you leave, it is gone.

Say what has changed, not just what is. 'Blood pressure is 96' is a number. 'Blood pressure was 140 on scene and is 96 now' is a diagnosis in progress. The trend is frequently more useful than the value, and only you have it.

And handover is not complete until somebody has accepted the patient. Not when you finished talking — when somebody took responsibility. Know their name, and write it down.
read.standard: Handover constitutes the transfer of clinical responsibility and represents the point of greatest information loss in the patient pathway. Structured formats reduce omission: SBAR comprises Situation, Background, Assessment and Recommendation; MIST comprises Mechanism, Injuries, Signs and Treatment and is commonly applied in trauma. Where service policy specifies a format, shared structure confers greater benefit than individual preference. Handover requires the receiving clinician's attention to be established and confirmed prior to commencement; delivery to an inattentive recipient does not constitute transfer. Handover is delivered once to the accepting clinician rather than in fragments to multiple recipients. Content should include information unavailable to the receiving facility: scene findings, patient position and duration, environmental conditions, medication packaging, and collateral history. Trends are reported alongside current values, as change carries greater diagnostic weight and is uniquely available to the transporting crew. Transfer is complete only on acceptance by a receiving clinician, whose identity should be recorded.

eli_new.analogy: The monitor gives them the numbers and the examination gives them the injuries. The only thing they cannot get without you is the room you found the patient in.
eli_new.body: The most valuable ninety seconds of a handover is the part nobody asks for: what the scene looked like. Nobody at the hospital will ever see that house, and once you drive away, everything you noticed in it disappears unless you said it out loud.

teach.prompt: Explain why handover matters, name a structure, and say what only you can contribute.

must_hit.point: Most information loss in a patient's journey happens at handover

MIST: Mechanism, Injuries, Signs, Treatment
Establish the recipient's attention before starting
Give it once, to the person taking over
Include the scene and collateral history — what they cannot get without you
Report trends, not just current values
Handover is complete only on acceptance — know the name

story.title: Since yesterday
story.dispatch: Handover — elderly female, found on the floor at home.
story.body:
The vital signs were all handed over accurately and the injuries were described precisely, and it was a good clean handover.

Nobody said she had been on that floor since the previous afternoon, or that the heating had been off.

The monitor could tell them everything except the only thing that mattered about the last eighteen hours.

B — BACKGROUND: the history that matters to this problem
A — ASSESSMENT: what you found, including vital signs and their trend
R — RECOMMENDATION: what you think they need
S — SIGNS: vital signs AND the trend
T — TREATMENT: what you did and how they responded
AND THE PART NO STRUCTURE PROMPTS: the scene. What you saw that nobody at hospital ever will.

concepts.title: Therapeutic communication and special communication needs
key_points: How you communicate changes what the patient tells you, and therefore what you find
Get to their eye level, use their name, introduce yourself, and say what you are going to do
Ask open questions first and narrow down, rather than starting with a list of yes or no questions
Allow silence — people fill it, and what they fill it with is often the important part
Do not interrupt early: patients who are allowed to finish give more useful histories
For hearing impairment: face them, make sure your face is visible and lit, speak normally rather than shouting, and write things down
For visual impairment: say who you are and who else is there, describe what is about to happen, and say when you are touching them
For limited English: use a professional interpreter service where available, and avoid using family members for clinical detail where possible
For cognitive or developmental difference: ask the person who knows them what normally works, and follow it
misconceptions: Shouting at a patient with hearing loss
Talking about a patient in front of them as though they are not there
Using a child as an interpreter for a parent
Standing over a patient while asking them to trust you

read.plain:
Communication is not a soft skill sitting beside the clinical work. It is the instrument you use to gather the history, and the history is most of the diagnosis. How you talk changes what you are told, which changes what you find.

Start with position. Get down to their eye level. A person standing over you is an authority figure; a person sitting at your level is somebody you talk to. Kneeling beside an armchair rather than looming over it changes the conversation measurably.

Say who you are and what you do. Use their name, and use the name they want — ask, rather than defaulting to a first name with an eighty-year-old. And say what you are going to do before you do it, every time.

Ask open questions first. 'Tell me what happened' produces more than 'did it start suddenly?' Start wide, then narrow. Closed questions are for pinning down detail once you know roughly where you are.

Then allow silence. This is the hardest one, because silence is uncomfortable and the instinct is to fill it with another question. People fill silences themselves, and what they fill them with is often the thing they were working up to. Count to three before you speak again.

And do not interrupt. Patients who are allowed to finish give better histories, and they take less time overall than patients who are steered from the first sentence.

Some specific situations.

Hearing impairment: face them, make sure your face is visible and lit, and speak normally rather than shouting — shouting distorts your mouth and makes lip-reading harder. Reduce background noise if you can. Write things down. Ask what works for them, because they know.

Visual impairment: say who you are as you arrive and who else is in the room. Describe what is about to happen. Say when you are about to touch them, every time, because being touched without warning when you cannot see it coming is frightening.

Limited English: use a professional interpreter service where one is available. Avoid relying on family for clinical detail where you can, and particularly avoid using children — they mistranslate, they are put in an impossible position, and the patient may not say the true thing in front of them.

Cognitive or developmental difference: the person who knows them usually knows what works. Ask. And talk to the patient, not only about them — talking about somebody in front of them as though they are not there is one of the most common and least noticed failures in this job.
read.standard: Communication technique determines the quality of history obtained and consequently the accuracy of assessment. Positioning at patient eye level alters the interaction from authority-based to collaborative. Providers introduce themselves, establish the patient's preferred form of address, and describe interventions before performing them. Open questioning precedes closed questioning, producing greater volume of relevant information; closed questions serve to clarify detail subsequently. Tolerance of silence permits patient elaboration, frequently yielding significant information. Premature interruption reduces history quality without reducing total encounter duration. Hearing impairment requires facial visibility and illumination, normal speech volume as shouting distorts articulation and impedes lip-reading, background noise reduction and written communication. Visual impairment requires verbal identification of providers present, description of intended actions and announcement prior to physical contact. Limited English proficiency requires professional interpretation where available; family interpretation is avoided for clinical content, and paediatric interpretation is specifically inappropriate. Cognitive and developmental difference requires consultation with familiar carers regarding effective approach, with communication directed to the patient rather than exclusively about them.

eli_new.analogy: The history is most of the diagnosis, and how you ask is the instrument you gather it with. A blunt instrument gathers less.
eli_new.body: Count to three before filling a silence. It feels much longer than it is, and the thing people say after that pause is very often the thing they had been deciding whether to tell you.

teach.prompt: Describe the techniques that improve history-taking and how you adapt for sensory impairment.

Open questions first, then narrow to closed
Allow silence and do not interrupt
Hearing impairment: face them, normal volume not shouting, write things down
Visual impairment: say who is there, describe actions, warn before touching
Limited English: professional interpreter, not children
Cognitive difference: ask the person who knows them, and talk TO the patient

story.title: Three seconds
story.dispatch: Medic 7 — 66-year-old female, vague abdominal discomfort, two days.
story.body:
She gave a short answer and stopped, and the student had the next question ready and did not ask it.

After about three seconds she said 'and I've been passing black stools since Tuesday', which she had not mentioned to anybody.

That sentence was the whole call, and it existed in a silence somebody nearly filled.

exam_favorites: The three jobs a report does

read.plain:
A patient care report does three jobs at once, and each one shapes how you write it.

It is a clinical document. The next clinician reads it to understand what happened before they arrived — sometimes immediately, sometimes days later when the patient deteriorates and somebody goes back to see what they were like at the start.

It is a legal document. If anything is ever questioned, this is the record. It may be read years later by people who were not there, and it will be the only account of what you found and why you did what you did.

And it is data. Aggregated across thousands of calls it is what quality improvement runs on, and vague reports make that process blind.

What goes in it: what you observed, and what you did, with times.

Times deserve emphasis. A blood pressure is a number. A blood pressure with a time beside it, next to another one twenty minutes later, is a trend, and the trend is frequently the clinically important thing. Times are what turn a list of observations into a story.

Write objectively. Record what you saw, heard, measured and were told. Not what you concluded about it. 'Patient was aggressive' is your interpretation; 'patient shouted, swore, and pushed the trolley away' is what happened, and it lets somebody else form their own view. The second is more useful and far more defensible.

Quote the patient where their words matter. 'I can't breathe' in quotation marks is stronger evidence than 'complained of breathlessness', and in a refusal it may be the most important line in the document.

The practical rule everybody quotes: if it is not written down, the assumption afterwards is that it did not happen. That is not quite fair — plenty of things happen and go unrecorded — but it is how it works in practice when somebody is reconstructing a call from paper.

Which is why pertinent negatives matter. If you specifically looked for something and it was not there, write that down. 'No chest pain' and 'abdomen soft and non-tender' are findings, because they record that you looked. A report that omits them looks identical to a report written by somebody who never checked.

And write it as though a stranger will read it in three years with no other source. Not your crewmate, who was there. A stranger, later, who has nothing else. That standard produces a report that does all three jobs.
read.standard: The patient care report functions simultaneously as a clinical document informing continuing care, a legal record subject to subsequent scrutiny, and a data source for quality improvement. Clinical continuity requires that subsequent providers can reconstruct the prehospital course, potentially at temporal remove. Legal function requires that the record support the reasoning behind decisions to readers without direct knowledge, potentially years later. Content comprises observations and interventions with associated times; temporal annotation converts discrete observations into trends, which frequently carry greater clinical significance than isolated values. Documentation is objective, recording observed, measured and reported information rather than interpretive conclusion; behavioural description is preferred to characterisation. Patient statements of significance are recorded verbatim within quotation marks, particularly in refusal documentation. Undocumented care is presumptively treated as not performed during retrospective reconstruction. Pertinent negatives are recorded, as documented absence of a specifically sought finding evidences examination; omission is indistinguishable from failure to assess. The standard for composition is comprehensibility to an unfamiliar reader at significant temporal remove without supplementary sources.

eli_new.analogy: Write it for a stranger reading it in three years with nothing else to go on. That is not a worst case. That is the actual reader.
eli_new.body: Pertinent negatives are the bit people skip. Writing 'abdomen soft and non-tender' takes four seconds and records that you looked. A report without it is indistinguishable from one written by somebody who never examined the abdomen at all.

story.title: Nobody could tell
story.dispatch: Records review — abdominal pain call, three years earlier.
story.body:
The crew had examined the abdomen carefully. Both of them remembered doing it, and neither could prove it.

The report recorded the vital signs and the transport and said nothing about the abdomen at all.

On paper, a careful examination that found nothing looks exactly like no examination.

concepts.title: Documentation errors, corrections and falsification
key_points: Errors in records are normal and expected; how they are corrected is what matters
On paper, draw a single line through the error so it remains readable, write the correction, and initial and date it
Never obliterate, scribble out, erase or use correction fluid — a record that cannot be read looks like concealment
On electronic records, use the system's amendment function, which keeps the original and records who changed what and when
Late entries are acceptable and should be labelled as such, with the time of the entry as well as the time of the event
Falsification means recording something that did not happen, omitting something that did, or altering a record to change its meaning
Falsification is a career-ending and potentially criminal act, and it is treated far more seriously than the error being hidden
The instinct to tidy a record after a bad outcome is the single most dangerous instinct in documentation

read.plain:
Everybody makes errors in records. The error is not the problem. How it is corrected is the entire subject.

On paper, the method is specific. Draw one single line through the mistake, so that what was originally written is still readable. Write the correction beside or above it. Initial it and date it.

The reason the original must stay readable is important: a correction you can still read is transparent, and a correction you cannot read looks like concealment. Never scribble something out into a black block. Never use correction fluid. Never erase. Those three actions turn an ordinary mistake into something that looks like hiding — and the appearance is what causes the problem, regardless of what you actually intended.

On electronic records, use the system's amendment function. It exists precisely for this: it preserves the original, records the change, and logs who made it and when. Do not work around it, and do not ask somebody else to amend under their login.

Late entries are legitimate. Sometimes you remember something afterwards, or information arrives later. Add it, label it clearly as a late entry, and record both times — when the thing happened, and when you wrote it. A labelled late entry is unremarkable. An unlabelled one that appears to have been written contemporaneously is a serious problem.

Falsification is different in kind, not degree. It means recording something that did not happen. Omitting something that did. Altering a record so that it means something other than the truth. Back-dating. Recording observations you did not take.

It is a career-ending act, it can be criminal, and here is the thing worth understanding: it is treated far more seriously than whatever was being hidden. A missed observation is a clinical error, and clinical errors are survivable, reportable and learnable. A falsified record is dishonesty, and dishonesty is not survivable in a clinical profession.

Which brings us to the most dangerous instinct in documentation: the urge to tidy a record once you learn the outcome was bad. It feels like clarifying. It feels like making sure the record properly reflects what you really did. It is not, and electronic systems log it, and it converts a defensible clinical situation into an indefensible one.

If you realise a report is wrong — even badly wrong, even in a way that reflects poorly — correct it properly, label it, and tell somebody. An honest correction, made openly, is defensible. Almost nothing else is.
read.standard: Documentation errors are anticipated; correction methodology determines acceptability. Paper records are corrected by a single strike-through preserving legibility of the original entry, with the correction, initials and date appended. Obliteration, erasure and correction fluid are contraindicated, as illegibility of the original creates an appearance of concealment irrespective of intent. Electronic records are amended through system amendment functions, which preserve original content and record the identity, nature and timing of modification; circumvention and amendment under another user's credentials are prohibited. Late entries are legitimate, requiring explicit labelling with both the time of the event and the time of entry; unlabelled retrospective entry constitutes a serious deficiency. Falsification comprises recording events that did not occur, omitting events that did, altering records to change meaning, back-dating, and recording unperformed observations. Falsification carries career and potential criminal consequence and is regarded more seriously than the underlying matter concealed, as clinical error is remediable while dishonesty is not. Retrospective record modification following adverse outcome constitutes the principal documentation hazard and is logged by electronic systems. Errors identified subsequently are corrected by the prescribed method with disclosure.

eli_new.analogy: A single line through a mistake is a correction anybody can read. A black block is a correction nobody can read, and the difference between those two is the difference between a mistake and a cover-up.
eli_new.body: The dangerous moment is learning that the patient did badly and feeling the urge to make the record clearer. That urge is not about clarity. Electronic systems log every keystroke, and it turns a survivable clinical error into an unsurvivable integrity problem.

story.title: Making it clearer
story.dispatch: Investigation — electronic record amended fourteen hours after a call.
story.body:
The original report was adequate. Not beautiful, but adequate, and it recorded a defensible clinical decision.

When he heard the patient had died, he went back in and added detail to make his reasoning clearer, which felt like the responsible thing to do.

The system logged the time of every keystroke. The clinical decision had been defensible. The edit was not.
